title: Local MAP Sampling for Diffusion Models
claim: Our framework subsumes and unifies existing approaches, and differs from standard unconditional generation only by replacing the posterior mean with a conditional MAP estimate.
layout: 3 panels: Venn diagram left, two stacked flow diagrams right; color-coded modules
description: The figure has three panels. Panel (a), on the left, is a Venn-style diagram of nested and overlapping green ellipses. LMAPS is a large ellipse that overlaps DPS and its variant, and DAPS sits outside it. Inside, red rounded boxes group TMPD with DDNM and an 'Optimization-based methods' group with DiffPIR and DCDP, which are drawn as blue ovals. Panels (b) and (c) on the right are stacked flow diagrams. Each runs a chain x_T → … → x_t → … → x_0 along the top. A module below computes an estimate and feeds a step function g, with Gaussian noise ε as another input. In (b) the estimate is the posterior mean E[x0|xt], shown in a green oval. In (c) it is the MAP estimate x0* ≈ argmax p(x0|xt,y), shown in an orange oval with a yellow measurement node y feeding it. The orange and green ovals make the contrast the main focus.
caption: Comparison of LMAPS with other methods. (a). The relationship between different alignment approaches; (b). The generation process of unconditional diffusion model; (c). The generation process of LMAPS.
abstract: Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) provides a principled Bayesian approach to inverse problems by sampling from $p(x_0 \mid y)$. While posterior sampling is valuable for capturing uncertainty and multi-modality, many classical and practical inverse problem settings ultimately prioritize accurate point estimation -- most notably the MAP estimator, which has long served as a standard reconstruction objective in imaging and scientific applications. We introduce Local MAP Sampling (LMAPS), a new inference framework that iteratively solves local MAP subproblems along the diffusion trajectory. This perspective clarifies their connection to global MAP and DPS, offering a unified probabilistic interpretation for optimization-based methods. Building on this foundation, we develop practical algorithms with a covariance approximation motivated by a Gaussian prior assumption, and a reformulated objective for stability and interpretability. Across a broad set of image restoration and scientific tasks, LMAPS achieves state-of-the-art performance.
